thread.title: Not at scale. The David here is 1/28th the size of the Golia

author: Paulo Santos
title: Not at scale. The David here is 1/28th the size of the Golia
text:
Not at scale. The David here is 1/28th the size of the Goliath. Please check actual size in a physical store, before ordering stock online. 
This is a headline you won’t read today, unless I write it. Yes, Amazon ( AMZN ) has just surpassed Apple ( AAPL ) for the title of “most valuable business on earth.” Looking only at market capitalization, you wouldn’t know that. Hence, you won’t be seeing it in headlines elsewhere.
However, a business’ value isn’t measured by market cap. Instead, it’s measured by EV (enterprise value), which removes the effect from how that business is financed. It so happens that Apple carries a lot of net cash, whereas Amazon.com carries a tiny bit of debt, and that makes all the difference. Consider the following:
What the market sees, with Amazon.com at $1,463.00 and Apple at $167.44, is that Amazon.com ’s diluted market capitalization is $722.7 billion, whereas Apple’s is still much larger at $875.9 billion. Again, that leads to no headlines. But Apple has $153.2 billion in net cash. As for Amazon.com, it carries $1.5 billion in net debt. Indeed, the difference would be larger still if we took into account Amazon.com’s extensive use of capital and operating leases. As a result of the above, as of today (and those quotes presented above), Apple had a $722.7 billion EV, vs. Amazon.com’s $724.2 billion. It was only today that Amazon.com ’s EV surpassed Apple’s. It was only today that Amazon.com became the most valuable business on earth. Amazon.com surpassing Apple is in and of itself news. It also speaks about how differently the market values these two companies, and indeed how news impact them so differently. But more on that later.
